title: Renting Isn't Throwing Money Away. Here's What Owning Really Costs
description:
In mid-October 2026 US asking rents fell on a year earlier for the thirty-eighth month in a row, while the thirty-year mortgage rate held at its highest level in nearly three years. So is renting still throwing money away?

We add up the money an owner never gets back (interest, property tax, upkeep and the lost return on the down payment), compare it with rent, and show how sharply the break-even moved when rates rose. Our honest take is at the end.
comment: Renter or owner? Tell us which one you are, and whether the maths in this video changes your mind.

Today that cost is about {{ latest(price) * (0.8 * latest(rate) + 0.2 * latest(bond) + 2) / 100 / 12 | usd }}, while the rent tenants pay rose only {{ pct_change(rent, "2021-01", "latest") | pct }}. So is renting still throwing money away, or is it now the owner who throws away more?

scenes.narration: On the fifteenth of October, two housing reports landed on the same day. Realtor.com said the typical asking rent in America's biggest cities was {{ latest(rent_news) | usd }} a month, down {{ -latest(rent_news_yoy) | pct1 }} on a year earlier. And Freddie Mac said the thirty-year mortgage rate was stuck at {{ latest(rate_news) | num }} percent, the highest in nearly three years.

headlines.text: Rents Rebound in AI Hubs and Affordable Alternatives: Realtor.com® September Rent Report
Average long-term US mortgage rate holds at 7.4%, remaining at highest level in nearly 3 years

scenes.narration: That is the {{ latest(rent_news_months) | num }}th month in a row that asking rents were lower than a year before. Meanwhile, a year ago the same mortgage cost {{ first(rate_news, "2025", "latest") | num }} percent. Renting got a little cheaper, and borrowing to buy got a lot more expensive.

chart.title: Rents slipping, mortgage rates at a three-year high
chart.label: WHAT JUST HAPPENED

scenes.narration: Which brings back the oldest argument at the family dinner table. Somebody always says that renting is throwing money away, because every month the rent is gone and you have nothing to show for it. Is that true? Today we will answer it the way an economist would. We will add up the money a renter never gets back, and the money an owner never gets back, using official data and a simple model. The answer depends mostly on one number, and it is the number that just hit a three-year high.

chart.title: Is renting really throwing money away?
chart.label: RENT VERSUS BUY, IN NUMBERS

scenes.narration: Here is the key idea. A renter loses the rent. But an owner also loses money every month, it just goes to different places: the bank, the tax office and the repair shop. The question is not who pays money they never see again. Both do. The question is who pays more.

chart.caption: Both renters and owners pay costs they never get back

scenes.narration: First, the long view. These three lines all start at one hundred in January 2000. The bottom one is all consumer prices, which rose {{ pct_change(cpi, "2000-01", "latest") | pct }}. The middle one is the rent that tenants actually pay, from the government's price index. It rose {{ pct_change(rent, "2000-01", "latest") | pct }}, faster than prices in general. And the top line is house prices from the Case-Shiller index, which follows the same homes as they sell again and again. They rose {{ pct_change(homes, "2000-01", "latest") | pct }}. So over a quarter of a century, owners did better than renters. That is where the dinner-table argument comes from.

chart.title: Rents, house prices and everything else
chart.subtitle: Index, January 2000 = 100

scenes.narration: But look at the shape of the lines. Rent climbs slowly and almost never falls. In the official index, it is still up {{ pct_change(rent, "2025-09", "latest") | pct1 }} on a year ago, even while asking rents for new leases slip, because the index covers every tenant, including those on old leases. House prices are much bumpier. From the peak in mid-2006 to early 2012, they fell {{ -pct_change(homes, "2006-07", "2012-02") | pct }}. Over the same years, rents rose {{ pct_change(rent, "2006-07", "2012-02") | pct }}. Anyone who bought at the top and had to sell at the bottom lost far more than a renter ever did. That is the first lesson of the data. A home is not only a place to live, it is also a big bet on one asset, in one town, usually made with borrowed money. Renting carries no such bet. When prices rise, owners win it. When they fall, renters are glad they never placed it.

chart.title: When house prices fell, rents kept rising
chart.subtitle: Index, July 2006 = 100

scenes.narration: So the honest comparison is not rent against nothing. It is rent against the costs of owning that you never get back.

chart.caption: Owners pay too: interest, tax and repairs

scenes.narration: Let's build that model with the median new home, which sells for {{ latest(price) | usd }} in the latest data. Assume a buyer puts twenty percent down and borrows the rest at today's rate. Four costs never come back. The first is interest on the loan, about {{ latest(price) * 0.8 * latest(rate) / 1200 | usd }} a month in the first year. The second is property tax, which we set at {{ 0.01 | pct }} of the price a year, about {{ latest(price) * 0.01 / 12 | usd }} a month. The third is upkeep, roofs, boilers and paint, also {{ 0.01 | pct }} a year. The fourth is easy to forget. The down payment could have earned interest instead. At the ten-year government bond yield of {{ latest(bond) | num }} percent, that lost return is about {{ latest(price) * 0.2 * latest(bond) / 1200 | usd }} a month. Add them up and owning this home throws away about {{ latest(price) * (0.8 * latest(rate) + 0.2 * latest(bond) + 2) / 100 / 12 | usd }} a month, before any rise in its price.

chart.title: What owning throws away each month
chart.subtitle: Median new home, twenty percent down, first year, before any price gain

scenes.narration: Notice what is not on that list. The mortgage payment itself is about {{ payment(0.8 * latest(price), latest(rate), 30) | usd }} a month, but part of it pays down the loan. That part is saving, not spending, because it builds up the share of the house you own. Interest is the part that is gone. In the early years of a thirty-year loan, interest is most of the payment, and only later does the balance start to shrink quickly. And interest is driven by one number, the mortgage rate. In January 2021 it was {{ value(rate, "2021-01") | num }} percent, close to the lowest ever recorded. Today it is {{ latest(rate) | num }} percent.

Now we can turn the model into a single break-even rent. If a similar home rents for less than this, renting is cheaper. If it rents for more, owning is cheaper. With the prices and rates of early 2000, the break-even was about {{ value(price, "2000-03") * (0.8 * value(rate, "2000-03") + 0.2 * value(bond, "2000-03") + 2) / 100 / 12 | usd }} a month. In early 2021, with higher prices but much lower rates, it was almost the same, about {{ value(price, "2021-01") * (0.8 * value(rate, "2021-01") + 0.2 * value(bond, "2021-01") + 2) / 100 / 12 | usd }}. Today it is about {{ latest(price) * (0.8 * latest(rate) + 0.2 * latest(bond) + 2) / 100 / 12 | usd }}. That is {{ latest(price) * (0.8 * latest(rate) + 0.2 * latest(bond) + 2) / 100 / 12 / (value(price, "2021-01") * (0.8 * value(rate, "2021-01") + 0.2 * value(bond, "2021-01") + 2) / 100 / 12) | times }} as much in a little over five years. Rents rose only {{ pct_change(rent, "2021-01", "latest") | pct }} over the same time. The break-even ran far ahead of rents.

chart.title: The break-even rent for the median new home
chart.subtitle: Monthly cost of owning that never comes back, before price gains

scenes.narration: There is one more piece, and it is the part owners love. If the house rises in value, that gain offsets the costs. On a log chart, where equal steps mean equal percentage growth, a straight line means a steady growth rate. Since 1987, house prices have grown about {{ cagr(homes, "1987-01", "latest") | pct1 }} a year on average. Rents, by comparison, grew about {{ cagr(rent, "1987-01", "latest") | pct1 }} a year. But the line is a trend, not a promise. Prices raced up before 2006, then fell hard for more than five years. A buyer only gets the average if they hold on through the bad years, and nobody knows in advance which years those will be.

chart.title: House prices and their long-run trend
chart.subtitle: Case-Shiller index, log scale, with a fitted growth line

scenes.narration: So let's give owners the benefit of the doubt and assume prices keep rising at that long-run pace. In early 2021, the costs of owning were then almost fully covered by the expected price gain, leaving about {{ value(price, "2021-01") * ((0.8 * value(rate, "2021-01") + 0.2 * value(bond, "2021-01") + 2) / 100 - cagr(homes, "1987-01", "latest")) / 12 | usd }} a month. That is why buying looked like a no-brainer back then. Today, even with the same price gain, owning the median new home still throws away about {{ latest(price) * ((0.8 * latest(rate) + 0.2 * latest(bond) + 2) / 100 - cagr(homes, "1987-01", "latest")) / 12 | usd }} a month. That is in the same range as the typical asking rent of {{ latest(rent_news) | usd }}, although that figure is mostly for apartments of up to two bedrooms, not new family houses. And the price gain is the shakiest part of the sum. Every one point of yearly price growth, more or less, moves the break-even by about {{ latest(price) * 0.01 / 12 | usd }} a month on this home.

chart.title: Break-even rent if prices keep rising
chart.subtitle: Unrecoverable cost of owning, minus the long-run yearly price gain

scenes.narration: So, is renting throwing money away? Not really. Renting throws away the rent. Owning throws away interest, tax, upkeep and the return your down payment could have earned. When rates were near record lows, the owner's losses were small and rising prices covered them, so buying usually won. Before price gains, a home was worth buying in early 2021 if it cost less than about {{ 1 / ((0.8 * value(rate, "2021-01") + 0.2 * value(bond, "2021-01") + 2) / 100) | num }} years of its own rent. Today, that line sits at about {{ 1 / ((0.8 * latest(rate) + 0.2 * latest(bond) + 2) / 100) | num }} years. Now that rates have more than doubled, the cost of owning has roughly doubled too, while asking rents for new leases have slipped over the past year. The same home, at the same rent, can flip from a good buy to a poor one just because the rate moved. Today, for many homes, renting is not the wasteful choice. It can be the cheaper one.

chart.title: Both throw money away. The rate decides who throws more.
chart.label: THE ANSWER

scenes.narration: Here is my take. The phrase throwing money away is wrong in both directions, and it pushes people into buying at the worst moments, when rates are high and they feel left behind. At today's rates, I think renting and investing the difference is a perfectly respectable choice, as long as the difference really does get invested. What would change my mind? A big drop in mortgage rates, or rents starting to climb fast again. And a caveat. These are national averages, and the model leaves out moving costs, insurance and tax breaks, so your own city and your own plans can tip the answer either way.

chart.title: Watch the rate, not the slogan
chart.label: MY TAKE

method: For the median new home with twenty percent down, we add first-year interest at the average thirty-year rate, the ten-year Treasury yield on the down payment, and one percent a year each for property tax and upkeep. We then subtract the average yearly rise in the Case-Shiller index since 1987 to show the case where prices keep growing.
